words.definition: To discover or bring to light something that was hidden or buried.
words.example: Renovating the old cottage, they unearthed a rusted tin packed with Victorian coins.
words.mnemonic: un- + earth — you take it out of the earth.

words.definition: To understand something complex or puzzling after careful thought.
words.example: No one could fathom why she abandoned a brilliant career at its very peak.
words.mnemonic: A fathom measures deep water; to fathom is to reach the deep bottom of an idea.

words.definition: To collect information or material gradually, a little at a time.
words.example: From scattered receipts, the detective gleaned the suspect's movements over the week.
words.mnemonic: Gleaners walked harvested fields picking up leftover grain one stalk at a time.

words.definition: To explore an area to gather information, especially about an enemy or terrain.
words.example: Two scouts crept ahead to reconnoiter the ridge before the column advanced.
words.mnemonic: Starts with 'recon' — the soldier's word for scouting ahead.

words.definition: To search deeply and thoroughly into a subject or source.
words.example: The biographer delved into dusty archives to trace the poet's forgotten childhood.
words.mnemonic: From Old English 'delfan', to dig — you dig down into a topic.

words.definition: To remove earth carefully in order to reveal buried remains or form a hole.
words.example: Archaeologists spent the whole summer excavating the buried Roman bathhouse.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out) + 'cave' — you hollow out a cave by digging.

words.definition: To find out something with certainty through checking or inquiry.
words.example: Doctors ran a battery of tests to ascertain the cause of her recurring fevers.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-CERTAIN' inside it — to make a thing certain.

words.definition: To make something clear and understandable, or to light it up brightly.
words.example: Her patient lecture illuminated a theory I had always found baffling.
words.mnemonic: il-LUMEN-ate — 'lumen' is Latin for light.

words.definition: A long journey, usually made by sea or through space.
words.example: The crew stocked the ship for a six-month voyage across the Pacific.
words.mnemonic: From French 'voie' (way, road) — a long trip along the way.

words.definition: A long, eventful journey full of changing fortunes and adventures.
words.example: Her decade-long odyssey through refugee camps finally ended in a quiet town.
words.mnemonic: From Homer's Odysseus, whose voyage home dragged on for ten years.

words.definition: A brief first attempt at an activity outside one's usual field.
words.example: The novelist's first foray into screenwriting genuinely surprised the critics.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'for a day' — a short venture out and back.

words.definition: A pleasing wide view, often seen through a long narrow opening.
words.example: From the mountain hut, a vista of glittering lakes opened up below them.
words.mnemonic: Italian for 'view', from 'vedere', to see.

words.definition: An unbroken view of a wide area surrounding the observer.
words.example: The rooftop bar offered a breathtaking panorama of the entire glittering city.
words.mnemonic: pan- (all) + Greek 'horama' (view) — an all-around view.

words.definition: Not yet mapped, explored, or recorded.
words.example: The submarine drifted into uncharted trenches no vessel had ever reached before.
words.mnemonic: un- + chart — a region with no chart (map) drawn for it yet.

words.definition: A position giving a good view of or advantage over something.
words.example: From his vantage on the hill, the general watched both armies wheel into place.
words.mnemonic: It's 'advantage' with the 'ad' dropped — a position of advantage.

words.definition: The likelihood or expectation that something will happen in the future.
words.example: The prospect of a promotion kept her working late every night.
words.mnemonic: PRO + SPECT (to look): you look forward pro-actively at what lies ahead.

words.definition: Eager to learn about things by asking many questions.
words.example: The inquisitive toddler opened every drawer and asked 'why?' a hundred times.
words.mnemonic: IN + QUIS (Latin 'to seek'): someone forever seeking answers, like a 'quiz' that never ends.

words.definition: An act of asking for information or a formal investigation.
words.example: After the crash, the government launched an inquiry into what went wrong.
words.mnemonic: Shares the root of 'query' and 'quest' (Latin quaerere, to seek) — a search for facts.

words.definition: Careful and detailed examination of something.
words.example: Her tax returns came under intense scrutiny from the auditors.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'SCREW-tiny': picture studying a tiny screw under a magnifying glass.

words.definition: The quality of being fresh, original, or unusual.
words.example: The novelty of the gadget wore off within a week, and it gathered dust.
words.mnemonic: From Latin novus, 'new' — the same root as 'novel' and 'innovate.'

words.definition: A person with deep knowledge or exceptional skill in a field.
words.example: The chess savant could recall every move of games played decades ago.
words.mnemonic: From French savoir, 'to know' — sounds like 'savvy,' someone who truly knows.

words.definition: A person respected for deep wisdom and sound judgment.
words.example: Villagers climbed the mountain to ask the old sage for advice.
words.mnemonic: Grey like the sage herb and a wise elder's beard — calm, seasoned, knowing.

words.definition: Produced or existing in very large amounts.
words.example: She offered profuse apologies, thanking everyone over and over.
words.mnemonic: PRO + FUSE (Latin fundere, to pour): liquids pouring out freely and overflowing.

words.definition: An overflowing, abundant supply of good things.
words.example: The autumn market was a cornucopia of pumpkins, apples, and squash.
words.mnemonic: The 'horn of plenty' (cornu = horn): a curved horn spilling out corn and fruit.

words.definition: A valuable collection of discovered or hidden items.
words.example: The dusty attic held a trove of rare coins and old love letters.
words.mnemonic: From 'treasure trove' — 'trove' comes from French trouver, to find.

words.definition: A large supply or store of something kept for later use.
words.example: Years of reading gave him a deep reservoir of obscure facts.
words.mnemonic: It holds water in RESERVE — 'reserve' + oir.

words.definition: A place or container where things are stored or kept.
words.example: The library serves as a repository for the town's historical records.
words.mnemonic: RE + POSIT (to place): the spot where you deposit and re-place things.

words.definition: A concise collection of detailed information on a subject.
words.example: The guidebook is a compendium of every hiking trail in the region.
words.mnemonic: 'Compile' + 'dium': knowledge compiled and weighed together into one handy volume.

words.definition: A large, heavy, and often scholarly book.
words.example: He lugged a thousand-page tome on medieval history to class.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'home' — so huge it could fill a whole home shelf by itself.

words.definition: A long, formal written work based on original research.
words.example: She spent three years writing her doctoral dissertation on bee behavior.
words.mnemonic: 'Discuss' at length: you dis-sert (set forth) a topic fully to earn a degree.

words.definition: A system for classifying things into ordered groups based on shared traits.
words.example: The biologist spent years refining the taxonomy that sorts beetles into families and genera.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'tax on me' — a government sorting citizens into income brackets is a classification scheme.

words.definition: The full stock of words known or used in a language or by one person.
words.example: Every new field forces you to learn its lexicon before the meetings start to make sense.
words.mnemonic: 'Lex' is Latin for word or law, plus 'icon' — a book full of word-icons.

words.definition: A formal system of names used within a particular field or discipline.
words.example: Chemistry's nomenclature turns a tangle of atoms into a single unambiguous name.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'nomen' (name) + 'clature' (to call) — literally the business of naming.

words.definition: A phrase whose meaning cannot be guessed from its individual words.
words.example: 'Kick the bucket' baffled the exchange student until someone explained the idiom meant to die.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'I dim' — the literal sense goes dim, and only the figurative one shines.

words.definition: A regional or social variety of a language with distinct words and pronunciation.
words.example: Her grandmother's mountain dialect used words the city cousins had never heard.
words.mnemonic: 'Dia-' (across) + 'lect' (speak) — how speech shifts as you move across a region.

words.definition: A fine, easily missed detail or a delicate distinction.
words.example: The joke's subtlety went over their heads, so nobody in the room laughed.
words.mnemonic: 'Subtle' hides a silent 'b' — the letter itself is a small detail you almost miss.

words.definition: A continuous sequence in which adjacent parts differ only slightly.
words.example: Gender, the professor argued, is better pictured as a continuum than as two boxes.
words.mnemonic: 'Continue' + 'um' — something that just keeps continuing with no breaks.

words.definition: The curved path an object or process follows through space or time.
words.example: After the promotion, her career's trajectory pointed straight toward the boardroom.
words.mnemonic: Say it 'tra-JET-ory' — picture a jet's arcing flight path across the sky.

words.definition: Including every possible detail; thoroughly complete.
words.example: The detective's exhaustive search left not a single drawer unopened.
words.mnemonic: Think 'exhaust' — you use up every option until the tank is empty.

words.definition: To seize a suspect in custody, or to grasp the meaning of something.
words.example: Officers moved quietly to apprehend the burglar before he reached the fence.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'app-a-hand' — a hand reaching out to grab a crook, or to grab an idea.

words.definition: To solve something complicated, or to come apart thread by thread.
words.example: It took three seasons for the show to unravel who the killer really was.
words.mnemonic: 'Un-' + 'ravel' — picture pulling one loose thread until the whole sweater comes apart.

words.definition: To explore or measure the full depth of something.
words.example: Years of therapy let him plumb feelings he had buried since childhood.
words.mnemonic: A plumber drops a lead 'plumb' weight on a line to measure how deep the water runs.

words.definition: To narrow a large group down to the best or essential few.
words.example: The committee had to winnow two hundred applicants down to a shortlist of five.
words.mnemonic: 'Winner' + 'now' — you keep the winners and let the wind blow the useless husks away.

words.definition: To search a place thoroughly, or to clean by hard rubbing.
words.example: They scoured the beach at dawn for the ring she had lost in the sand.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'scout' + 'hour' — you scout every inch of a place for an hour.

words.definition: To warn of or point toward something that will happen later.
words.example: The still, heavy air seemed to presage a violent storm before nightfall.
words.mnemonic: 'Pre-' (before) + 'sage' (a wise seer) — a sage who foretells before it happens.

words.definition: The good fortune of stumbling upon something valuable or delightful entirely by chance.
words.example: Finding my favorite bookshop while lost on a side street was pure serendipity.
words.mnemonic: From the fairy tale 'The Three Princes of Serendip,' who kept making lucky discoveries by accident.

words.definition: Occurring by a lucky, unplanned chance in a welcome and pleasant way.
words.example: Our serendipitous meeting at the airport gate grew into a lifelong friendship.
words.mnemonic: Same root as the Princes of Serendip — describes the moment a happy accident lands in your lap.

words.definition: Willing to take risks and eager to try daring or bold new things.
words.example: The venturesome hikers ignored the paved trail and scrambled up the unmarked ridge instead.
words.mnemonic: 'Venture' + '-some' — someone brimming with the urge to venture into the unknown.

words.definition: Showing signs that promise success or good things to come.
words.example: A bright, cloudless sky on moving day felt like an auspicious start to their new life.
words.mnemonic: From the Roman 'auspex,' a priest who read good omens in the flight of birds.

words.definition: Strongly shaping later developments by serving as an original source of ideas.
words.example: Darwin's seminal book reshaped how every biologist after him understood living things.
words.mnemonic: Shares its root with 'semen/seed' — a work that plants seeds which grow into a whole field.

words.definition: A sudden, striking realization that makes something confusing instantly clear.
words.example: Halfway through her shower, she had an epiphany about how to fix the broken ending.
words.mnemonic: Picture a light bulb flashing on — a tiny 'pip' of insight that suddenly illuminates everything.

words.definition: Never getting tired; able to keep going with seemingly endless energy.
words.example: The indefatigable nurse worked three straight shifts and never once lost her cheer.
words.mnemonic: Break it down: 'in-' (not) + 'defatigable' (able to be worn out) — literally cannot be exhausted.

words.definition: Extremely eager and enthusiastic about a particular interest or pursuit.
words.example: An avid reader, he devoured four thick novels during a single week of vacation.
words.mnemonic: 'Avid' sounds like 'have it' — an avid fan has simply GOT to have it.

words.definition: To feel a deep, aching desire for something or someone.
words.example: Stuck in the crowded city, she yearned for the quiet fields of her childhood.
words.mnemonic: 'Yearn' sounds like 'earn' — you long for it so badly you'd earn it any way you could.

words.definition: To reveal or make publicly known something that was previously hidden.
words.example: The mayor will unveil the new bronze statue at tomorrow morning's ceremony.
words.mnemonic: 'un-' + 'veil' — lift the veil off something to show what lies underneath.

words.definition: Remarkably great in size, amount, or degree; strikingly impressive.
words.example: The young pianist showed prodigious talent, mastering pieces that stumped seasoned adults.
words.mnemonic: Think 'prodigy' — a prodigy displays impressively enormous, jaw-dropping ability.
